items.readable_text:
Content:
The reciprocals of sine, cosine, and tangent are given special names:

Content:
- The reciprocal of sine is cosecant, abbreviated [MATH: \csc.]
[MATH: \csc(\theta) = \dfrac 1 {\sin(\theta)} = \dfrac 1 {\dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{hypotenuse}}} = \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{opposite}}]
- The reciprocal of cosine is secant, abbreviated [MATH: \sec.]
[MATH: \sec (\theta) = \dfrac 1 {\cos(\theta)} = \dfrac 1 {\dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{hypotenuse}}} = \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{adjacent}}]
- The reciprocal of tangent is cotangent, abbreviated [MATH: \cot.]
[MATH: \cot (\theta) = \dfrac 1 {\tan(\theta)} = \dfrac 1 {\dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{adjacent}}} = \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{opposite}}]

Content:
Let's write down expressions for [MATH: \csc(B),] [MATH: \sec(B),] and [MATH: \cot(B)] for the triangle below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/dd717bdb89a56d473f0e04333131efa3]

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\csc(B) &= \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac c b \[5pt]
\sec(B) &= \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{adjacent}} = \dfrac c a \[5pt]
\cot(B) &= \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac a b \
}]

We compute the three reciprocal trigonometric ratios as follows:

[MATH: \eqalign{ \csc\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac 5 3, \[5pt] \sec\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{adjacent}} = \dfrac 5 4, \[5pt] \cot\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta} = \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac 4 3. }]

items.readable_text:
Content:
If we are given two sides of a right triangle, how can we calculate the reciprocal ratios [MATH: \sec,] [MATH: \csc,] or [MATH: \cot] when we are missing one of the necessary sides in the ratio?

Content:
The trick here is the same that we use for finding [MATH: \sin,] [MATH: \cos,] or [MATH: \tan\mathbin{:}] we use the Pythagorean theorem for finding the missing side.

Content:
To illustrate, let's calculate [MATH: \csc L] in the triangle below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f1ab2997f0b0e6222a05b0a528ef3670]

Content:
Remember that [MATH: \csc] is the reciprocal of [MATH: \sin.] So first we need to compute sine:

Content:
[MATH: \sin L = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{JK}{KL} = \dfrac{JK}{4}]

Content:
To find the length [MATH: JK,] we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

Content:
[MATH: JK|= sqrt(KL^{2} − JL^{2}); = sqrt(4^{2} − 3^{2}); = sqrt(16 − 9); = sqrt(7)]

Content:
So we have

Content:
[MATH: \sin L = \dfrac{JK}{4} = \dfrac{ \sqrt{7} }{4},]

Content:
and therefore

Content:
[MATH: \csc L|= ((sqrt(7))/(4))^{− 1}; = (4)/(sqrt(7)); = (4 ⋅ sqrt(7))/(sqrt(7) ⋅ sqrt(7)); = (4sqrt(7))/(7).]

sections.normalized_html: Find [MATH: \sec L] for [MATH: \triangle KLJ] (shown below).
sections.readable_text:
Find [MATH: \sec L] for [MATH: \triangle KLJ] (shown below).

[IMG: /graphics/ec35a6fdb4b36e572e24bc5199fb77e5]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Remember that [MATH: \sec] is the reciprocal of [MATH: \cos.] So first we need to compute cosine:

[MATH: \cos L = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{JL}{KL} = \dfrac{JL}{5}]

To find the length [MATH: JL,] we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

[MATH: JL|= sqrt(KL^{2} − JK^{2}); = sqrt(5^{2} − 3^{2}); = sqrt(25 − 9); = sqrt(16); = 4]

So we have

[MATH: \cos L = \dfrac{JL}{5} = \dfrac{4}{5},]

and therefore

[MATH: \sec L|= ((4)/(5))^{− 1} = (5)/(4).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The reciprocals of sine, cosine, and tangent are given special names:

Content:
- The reciprocal of sine is cosecant, abbreviated [MATH: \csc.]
[MATH: \csc(\theta) = \dfrac 1 {\sin(\theta)} = \dfrac 1 {\dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{hypotenuse}}} = \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{opposite}}]
- The reciprocal of cosine is secant, abbreviated [MATH: \sec.]
[MATH: \sec (\theta) = \dfrac 1 {\cos(\theta)} = \dfrac 1 {\dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{hypotenuse}}} = \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{adjacent}}]
- The reciprocal of tangent is cotangent, abbreviated [MATH: \cot.]
[MATH: \cot (\theta) = \dfrac 1 {\tan(\theta)} = \dfrac 1 {\dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{adjacent}}} = \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{opposite}}]

Content:
Let's write down expressions for [MATH: \csc(B),] [MATH: \sec(B),] and [MATH: \cot(B)] for the triangle below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/dd717bdb89a56d473f0e04333131efa3]

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\csc(B) &= \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac c b \[5pt]
\sec(B) &= \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{adjacent}} = \dfrac c a \[5pt]
\cot(B) &= \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac a b \
}]

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratios and the Pythagorean Theorem

Content:
If we are given two sides of a right triangle, how can we calculate the reciprocal ratios [MATH: \sec,] [MATH: \csc,] or [MATH: \cot] when we are missing one of the necessary sides in the ratio?

Content:
The trick here is the same that we use for finding [MATH: \sin,] [MATH: \cos,] or [MATH: \tan\mathbin{:}] we use the Pythagorean theorem for finding the missing side.

Content:
To illustrate, let's calculate [MATH: \csc L] in the triangle below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f1ab2997f0b0e6222a05b0a528ef3670]

Content:
Remember that [MATH: \csc] is the reciprocal of [MATH: \sin.] So first we need to compute sine:

Content:
[MATH: \sin L = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{JK}{KL} = \dfrac{JK}{4}]

Content:
To find the length [MATH: JK,] we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

Content:
[MATH: JK|= sqrt(KL^{2} − JL^{2}); = sqrt(4^{2} − 3^{2}); = sqrt(16 − 9); = sqrt(7)]

Content:
So we have

Content:
[MATH: \sin L = \dfrac{JK}{4} = \dfrac{ \sqrt{7} }{4},]

Content:
and therefore

Content:
[MATH: \csc L|= ((sqrt(7))/(4))^{− 1}; = (4)/(sqrt(7)); = (4 ⋅ sqrt(7))/(sqrt(7) ⋅ sqrt(7)); = (4sqrt(7))/(7).]

---

Item 6 — Example: Evaluating a Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratio Given a Triangle Using the Pythagorean Theorem

Example Prompt:
Find [MATH: \sec L] for [MATH: \triangle KLJ] (shown below).

[IMG: /graphics/ec35a6fdb4b36e572e24bc5199fb77e5]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Remember that [MATH: \sec] is the reciprocal of [MATH: \cos.] So first we need to compute cosine:

[MATH: \cos L = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{JL}{KL} = \dfrac{JL}{5}]

To find the length [MATH: JL,] we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

[MATH: JL|= sqrt(KL^{2} − JK^{2}); = sqrt(5^{2} − 3^{2}); = sqrt(25 − 9); = sqrt(16); = 4]

So we have

[MATH: \cos L = \dfrac{JL}{5} = \dfrac{4}{5},]

and therefore

[MATH: \sec L|= ((4)/(5))^{− 1} = (5)/(4).]
